834.title: Jan Hus (1415)
834.hook: a Prague preacher burned at the Council of Constance, promised safe conduct
834.tomorrow: Thomas à Kempis in his cell
834.howItsDone: Jan Hus is remembered by Protestant churches as a forerunner of the Reformation and by the Moravian Church as part of its own story, and the Czech Republic marks a public day in his memory; the Catholic Church has expressed regret for his death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wycliffe's Bible, copied by hand so ordinary people could hear scripture in English, and your line was the ploughman's bible.

A promise, on paper, with a seal. That's what the preacher carries when he leaves Prague. He's been summoned to a great church council in Constance, to answer charges that his teaching is heresy. He has reason to be wary. But Sigismund, king and future emperor, has given him a letter of safe conduct: travel there, speak, and come home unharmed. So he goes, believing he'll be allowed to explain himself. Before long, he's in prison. Today: Jan Hus.

Hus was a priest and teacher in Prague, and he preached in a chapel there in Czech, the language of the people in the pews, not only in Latin. He'd read Wycliffe, whose followers we met yesterday, and shared some of his concerns: a church too tied to money and power, and scripture as the measure of it all. He preached hard against the sale of indulgences. Crowds came to hear him, and church authorities came to see him as dangerous. At Constance, the council demanded he take back a list of teachings. Hus answered that some of them he had never taught, and he couldn't swear to give up what he had never held, or deny what he believed true, unless someone showed him from scripture that he was wrong. The council judged him a heretic, and he was burned at the stake. Sigismund's safe conduct didn't save him. Christians remember Hus in different ways. Protestant histories have called him a forerunner of the Reformation, and the Moravian Church traces its roots to communities that grew from his followers. In the Czech lands he became a national figure. The Catholic Church, for its part, has in recent times expressed deep regret for his cruel death. Words handed down under his name urge a Christian to seek the truth, love it, speak it, hold to it and defend it to death. They echo Jesus in John's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free."
screen: `HE WOULD NOT DENY WHAT HE NEVER TAUGHT.`

segments.voice: Think of one promise you've made that has become inconvenient, to a friend, at work, at home, and notice how much easier it would be to drop it, especially if someone else dropped theirs; then choose to keep it. The Psalms describe the person who "sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not." If you pray, ask for the strength to keep your word; if not, hold the promise, and let it stay.
Jan Hus. A Prague preacher who would not deny what he believed true, and was burned at the Council of Constance despite a promise of safe conduct.
Your line: seek the truth. Even when a promise made to you breaks. Tomorrow, a quiet copyist.

835.title: Thomas à Kempis in his cell
835.hook: a quiet copyist-monk, and a small book on following Christ
835.carry: in a nook with a book
835.howItsDone: Christians of several traditions read The Imitation of Christ a short chapter at a time, often as part of a daily quiet time, and some copy out lines of scripture or devotional books by hand as a way of praying.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jan Hus held to what he believed true after a promise to him was broken, and your line was seek the truth.

Scratch, dip, scratch. A quill moving across parchment, a pot of ink, a window of gray light, and a man bent over a desk for hours, copying out the Bible letter by letter. No printing press here; if a monastery wanted a book, someone like him made it by hand. The house is a small community of canons near Zwolle, in what is now the Netherlands. The man rarely leaves. He prays with his brothers, copies books, guides the younger ones, and writes little pieces of his own. Nobody outside would call his life remarkable.

Thomas belonged to a movement called the Modern Devotion. Its idea was simple: a real, inner faith, lived out in ordinary days, by lay people and religious alike. Not great learning or grand projects, but prayer, humility, honest work, and walking after Christ. Out of that world came a small book, usually credited to Thomas, called The Imitation of Christ. Its chapters are short, sometimes a few lines, the kind you read in a minute and think about all day. It tells the reader to love being unknown, and to care more about living well than knowing a lot. It says, in effect, that a humble farmer who serves God is better off than a proud scholar who studies the stars and neglects himself. Its aim is in the title: to follow Christ closely, in the heart. The book went out without much fanfare, and in time found readers far beyond his house, Catholic and Protestant both. A saying handed down under Thomas's name is usually given in Latin as in angello cum libello: in a little nook with a little book. He looked for rest everywhere, it says, and found it only there. That's a copyist's line. The Bible has an older one. In Deuteronomy, a king is told that when he takes the throne, in the King James Bible, "he shall write him a copy of this law in a book". Not only hear it. Write it, by his own hand.

Find a pen and a scrap of paper, pick one line that matters to you, a verse, a prayer you know, a line from a book that stayed with you, and write it out slowly, letter by letter, at the speed of attention. When it's finished, read it once in silence. If you pray, let it become your prayer for the rest of the sit; if not, stay with the words on the page.
Kempis. The quiet copyist and canon of the Modern Devotion, Thomas à Kempis, to whom tradition credits The Imitation of Christ.
Your line: in a nook with a book. A small corner, and one good line. Rest easy, day eight hundred thirty-five.

836.title: Joan's trial
836.hook: asked if she was in God's grace: if I am not, may God put me there; if I am, may he keep me
836.howItsDone: Catholics honor Joan of Arc as a saint, and her answer about grace is quoted by Christians of different churches as a picture of humble trust before God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas à Kempis, copying in his quiet house, and your line was in a nook with a book.

Do you know if you are in the grace of God? The question comes across a crowded room in Rouen. Learned men in robes sit in rows: churchmen, doctors of theology, lawyers. Before them stands a young woman from a farming village, in chains between sessions, who cannot read. She has led soldiers in war, she says, because voices from God told her to. Now she's on trial for her life. And the question is a trap. If she says yes, she sounds proud, as if she could be sure of God's verdict. If she says no, she admits she's not in God's favor, and condemns herself.
screen: `ARE YOU IN THE GRACE OF GOD?`

segments.voice: Joan of Arc grew up in a village in France during a long war with England. She said saints' voices told her to help the French king. Somehow she got an audience with him, then an army, and she rode with it in armor. Later she was captured and handed over to a church court that sided with her enemies. The trial record survives. Take the moment over grace. As the record gives it, paraphrased: if I am not, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me there. She added that she'd be the saddest person in the world if she knew she were not in God's grace. The answer holds, but not by being clever. It doesn't claim to know what only God knows, and it doesn't confess what isn't true. It turns the trap into a prayer. In the New Testament, grace is a gift nobody earns. Ephesians puts it this way in the King James Bible: "For by grace are ye saved through faith". Her answer leaves grace where that verse puts it: in God's hands. Jesus had told his followers what to do when brought before councils: "take no thought how or what ye shall speak: for it shall be given you in that same hour". The court condemned her, and she was burned. Years later, a new church inquiry overturned the verdict, and in time the Catholic Church named her a saint.
screen: `IF I AM NOT, MAY GOD PUT ME THERE.`
`IT SHALL BE GIVEN YOU IN THAT HOUR.`

segments.voice: Think of a question once put to you as a trap, where yes and no both lose. In your mind, try Joan's way: not proving them wrong, not giving in, but a short answer honest about what you don't know and humble about what you do. If you pray, ask for the right words when the moment comes; if not, rest in the not-knowing for a while.
Joan's trial. The church court in Rouen where a young woman from a farming village answered a trap about God's grace with a humble prayer.
Your line: if I am, keep me. A trap, turned into a prayer. Day eight hundred thirty-six, finished.

837.title: Constantinople falls (1453)
837.hook: the last liturgy in Hagia Sophia; the Orthodox world's center shifts north
837.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians remember the fall of Constantinople with sorrow, and the Ecumenical Patriarch, honored by Orthodox Christians as first among their patriarchs, still has his seat in the city, now Istanbul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joan's trial: a trap about God's grace, answered with a humble prayer. Your line was if I am, keep me.

Candles, a great dome overhead, and a crowd with every reason to be afraid. The city is under siege. Outside, an army has pounded the walls with cannon, day after day. On the last evening, the old accounts say, the people of Constantinople crowd into their great church for one more service. Greek Christians and Latin Christians, who had quarreled bitterly, stand under the same dome and pray together. Some confess their sins. Some ask forgiveness of the person next to them. Then the soldiers go back to the walls.

The church was Hagia Sophia, Holy Wisdom, long the heart of Eastern Christianity: the seat of the patriarch, the place where emperors were crowned. The army outside belonged to the Ottoman sultan, Mehmed. When the walls broke, the emperor, Constantine, died fighting at them, the accounts say, and the city that called itself the new Rome passed into Ottoman hands. Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia, and before long it was a mosque, with Muslim prayer under the same dome. People still tell a story about that last liturgy. As soldiers burst in, the story goes, a priest at the altar picked up the holy gifts and walked into the wall, and the wall closed behind him. One day, the story says, he will walk out and finish the service. It's told as legend, not history: the kind of story people tell when something unfinished hurts. A Psalm knows that hurt. In the King James Bible: "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion." But the Orthodox world didn't end; its center moved. In the north, Russian Christians began to see themselves as carriers of what Constantinople had held, and some in Moscow spoke of a third Rome. And in the old city, Christians stayed. The patriarchate went on, with a new patriarch installed under the new rulers, and the Orthodox lived as a minority, keeping their churches and their liturgy, generation after generation. The last liturgy in Hagia Sophia was not the last liturgy.
screen: `THE PRIEST WHO WALKED INTO THE WALL.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind Christians who live as a small community, among neighbors who mostly follow another faith or none: a small church on an ordinary street, a few families keeping it going year after year. If you know one by name, bring it to mind. If you pray, pray for them; if you don't, simply wish them well, and their neighbors too.
Constantinople falls. The great Christian city of the East passes to the Ottomans, Hagia Sophia becomes a mosque, and Orthodox Christians carry on, in the old city and in the north.
Your line: the last liturgy. The city fell, and the people who prayed there kept going. Day eight hundred thirty-seven, done.

838.title: Gutenberg's Bible
838.hook: a goldsmith's press in Mainz prints the Bible, and books start to get cheap
838.howItsDone: Christians often give Bibles as gifts at baptisms, confirmations, weddings and graduations, and Bible societies print and give away Bibles in many languages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantinople fell, and the last liturgy under the great dome turned out not to be the last. Your line was the last liturgy.

A tiny metal letter, the size of a fingernail, stands on its end. A capital I. Next to it, an n. Then another, and another, until a whole line sits in a wooden frame, backward, like a word seen in a mirror. Ink goes over it, paper comes down, a screw turns, and the page comes up with the words the right way round. Then the letters come apart and get set again for the next page. In a workshop in the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg is doing this with the whole Bible.

Before the press, every Bible in Europe was copied by hand, the way Thomas à Kempis copied at his desk. Every copy was its own work, and precious. Gutenberg's idea was to make the letters movable: cast them in metal, line them up, print a page, then break them apart and use them again. His Bible was in Latin, the Bible the Western church read in worship. Its Genesis begins with the words the King James Bible gives as: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The pages were made to look like the best handwritten books: two columns, dark, even letters. Copies were often finished by hand, with red headings and painted capitals, so no two look quite the same. Then other presses followed, in other cities. Books got cheaper, and more people could own one. Later, reformers would print the Bible in German and English, in the languages people spoke at home, and tracts and sermons traveled fast. Christians argued, sometimes fiercely, over what all those readers should do with what they read. But the change underneath was simple. A Psalm says, "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." For a long time, that lamp sat in a church or a library. The press began to put it on kitchen tables.
screen: `COPIED BY HAND, ONE AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Think of a book that changed something for you: maybe a Bible, a novel, or a book of poems someone handed you at the right time. Then think of one person who might need a book right now, a friend, a child, a coworker, someone on your street, and choose a book for them. If you pray, pray for them as you choose; if you don't, just hold them in mind.
Gutenberg's Bible. The Latin Bible printed with movable metal type in Mainz, part of a change that made books, and Bibles, cheaper to own.
Your line: words for everyone. Once one press worked, others followed, in other cities. See you tomorrow.

839.title: Lalibela
839.hook: in Ethiopia, churches carved downward out of solid rock
839.howItsDone: Ethiopian Orthodox Christians make pilgrimage to Lalibela, especially at Genna, their Christmas, and at Timkat, the feast of Jesus's baptism, gathering in white shawls in the rock-cut churches to pray and sing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gutenberg's Bible: metal letters, set and reset, that made books cheaper to own. Your line was words for everyone.

On a plain of reddish stone in the Ethiopian highlands, at first there's nothing to see. Then the ground opens. At the bottom of a deep trench, its roof level with the plain, stands a church: doors, windows and a cross on top, all one piece with the rock around it. Nobody built it up. Somebody dug it down. Pilgrims in white shawls climb down stone steps into the trenches to pray.

Lalibela is a town in northern Ethiopia, named for a king the Ethiopian Orthodox Church honors as a saint. Tradition says King Lalibela wanted a holy city in his own land, a new Jerusalem, for Christians who couldn't make the long journey to the old one. And so, the tradition goes, churches were cut out of the living rock. The carvers started from the top. They cut a trench around a huge block of stone, leaving it standing free, then hollowed it from inside: rooms, pillars, arches, windows, nothing added. Cut away too much, and there was no putting it back. One church is shaped like a cross when seen from above, its roof flat with the ground. The place carries names from the Holy Land; a stream there is called the Jordan. Ethiopian Christianity has its own way. Its church belongs to the family of Oriental Orthodox churches, with its own language of worship, Ge'ez, its own calendar and its own feasts. At Christmas, which Ethiopian Christians call Genna, crowds of pilgrims fill the trenches and the rock-cut courtyards. Isaiah has a line that fits, in the King James Bible: "look unto the rock whence ye are hewn." And Jesus, in Matthew, says, "upon this rock I will build my church." At Lalibela, that image becomes stone you can touch. The church isn't set on the rock. It is the rock.
screen: `CUT FROM THE TOP, HOLLOWED FROM INSIDE.`
`NOT ON THE ROCK. IT IS THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: The carvers at Lalibela made room by taking away. Look at the week ahead and find one hour you could cut free, the way they cut a trench around a block of stone: early in the morning, a lunch break, an evening without a screen. If you pray, that hour can be for prayer; if you don't, let it be for quiet, a walk, or a long look at something beautiful.
Lalibela. A town in Ethiopia, named for a saint-king, where churches were carved down into solid rock as a new Jerusalem.
Your line: churches in the rock. Sometimes room is made by taking away. That was day eight hundred thirty-nine.

840.title: Nubia's churches
840.hook: Christian kingdoms once flourished on the Nile in what is now Sudan, and their churches were almost forgotten
840.howItsDone: The Nubian churches no longer hold services, but paintings from the cathedral at Faras are kept in museums, and Christians in Sudan and elsewhere sometimes remember the Nubian kingdoms as part of their own story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lalibela, where churches were carved down into solid rock. Your line was churches in the rock.

Sand, blown over the ruins of a town by the Nile. Archaeologists dig, and under the sand they find walls, and on the walls, faces. Saints with large dark eyes. Angels. Mary holding her child. A bishop in his robes, looking straight out at them as if he'd been waiting. These are the walls of a cathedral at Faras, in old Nubia, the land along the Nile south of Egypt. Whole Christian kingdoms once lived here, and their names had mostly faded from memory.

The Bible already knows this land, though it calls it Ethiopia, its word for the country south of Egypt. A Psalm says, in the King James Bible, "Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God." And in Acts, Philip meets on the road "a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians." He's reading Isaiah; he asks to be baptized, and goes on his way rejoicing. Some readers place his queen's kingdom in the land later called Nubia. Later, kings along the Nile became Christian. Their kingdoms, Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia, built churches and cathedrals, with bishops, monasteries and walls covered in paintings. They worshiped in Greek and Coptic, and wrote in their own Nubian language too. For a long time they flourished. Then, slowly, the kingdoms weakened and the churches emptied. There was no single dramatic fall, the way there was at Constantinople. The faith faded out of the valley, and sand covered the walls. Christian history isn't only Rome, Constantinople and the cathedrals of Europe. It reached Africa early, riding home with that traveler from Philip's road, and it grew along the Nile. This week ran from Jan Hus seeking the truth, through Thomas à Kempis in his nook, Joan's humble answer, the last liturgy, Gutenberg's letters and the rock churches of Lalibela, to faces under the sand. To remember a church is to say: these people were here, and they prayed.

Say the kingdoms' names slowly, once each, Nobadia, Makuria, Alodia, and then the town, Faras. Picture the painted bishop on the wall, the saints with their wide eyes, and the people who once stood before them on an ordinary morning; you don't know their names, but you can hold them for a minute anyway. If you pray, give thanks for them; if you don't, let the names be enough.
Nubia's churches. The churches of the Christian kingdoms on the Nile, in what is now Sudan, which faded and were found again under the sand.
Your line: remembered churches. A name said aloud is a name remembered. Eight hundred forty days now.
